claim: The neocortex is organized around layered microcircuits consisting of a variety of excitatory and inhibitory neuronal types which perform rate- and oscillation-based computations.
source: The neocortex is organized around layered microcircuits consisting of a variety of excitatory and inhibitory neuronal types which perform rate- and oscillation-based computations.
evidence: This is a general statement about neocortical organization that draws from established neuroscience knowledge.

claim: Both superficial and deep layers of the primary mouse visual cortex implement two ultrasensitive and bistable switches built on mutual inhibitory connectivity motives between somatostatin, parvalbumin, and vasoactive intestinal polypeptide cells.
source: Using modeling, we show that both superficial and deep layers of the primary mouse visual cortex implement two ultrasensitive and bistable switches built on mutual inhibitory connectivity motives between somatostatin, parvalbumin, and vasoactive intestinal polypeptide cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the computational modeling study presented in the manuscript.

claim: The switches toggle pyramidal neurons between high and low firing rate states that are synchronized across layers through translaminar connectivity.
source: The switches toggle pyramidal neurons between high and low firing rate states that are synchronized across layers through translaminar connectivity.
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling study about the functional consequences of the switches.

claim: Inhibited and disinhibited states are characterized by low- and high-frequency oscillations, respectively, with layer-specific differences in frequency and power which show asymmetric changes during state transitions.
source: Moreover, inhibited and disinhibited states are characterized by low- and high-frequency oscillations, respectively, with layer-specific differences in frequency and power which show asymmetric changes during state transitions.
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling study about oscillatory properties of different circuit states.

claim: The majority of interneurons can be assigned to biochemically defined classes, such as parvalbumin (PV), somatostatin (SST), and vasoactive intestinal polypeptide (VIP) positive cells.
source: The majority of interneurons can be assigned to biochemically defined classes, such as parvalbumin (PV), somatostatin (SST), and vasoactive intestinal polypeptide (VIP) positive cells (Tremblay et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Tremblay et al., 2016.

claim: These neurons are distributed across layers and connected according to an intricate circuit diagram with intra- and interlaminar connections.
source: These neurons are distributed across layers and connected according to an intricate circuit diagram with intra- and interlaminar connections (Pfeffer et al., 2013; Jiang et al., 2015; Kätzel et al., 2011; Harris and Shepherd, 2015; Cardin, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: The discovery of regularities within the connectivity pattern of excitatory and inhibitory neurons prompted researchers to propose the existence of canonical microcircuits.
source: The discovery of regularities within the connectivity pattern of excitatory and inhibitory neurons prompted researchers to propose the existence of canonical microcircuits (Douglas and Martin, 2004; Beul and Hilgetag, 2014), which implement elementary computations that are repeated across the brain (Miller, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Douglas and Martin, 2004; Beul and Hilgetag, 2014; and Miller, 2016.

claim: Disinhibitory subcircuits release pyramidal neurons from strong inhibition.
source: These studies have not only highlighted an essential role of inhibitory neurons to balance excitation, but also recognized disinhibitory subcircuits, which release pyramidal neurons from strong inhibition (Fishell and Kepecs, 2020; Letzkus et al., 2015; Pi et al., 2013; Walker et al., 2016; Jackson et al., 2016; Fu et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: Neuronal oscillations in different frequency bands have been attributed to the activity of different interneuron types.
source: Moreover, neuronal oscillations in different frequency bands have been attributed to the activity of different interneuron types (Cardin et al., 2009; Sohal et al., 2009; Chen, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Cardin et al., 2009; Sohal et al., 2009; and Chen, 2017.

claim: The dynamics of more complex networks comprising multiple layers with translaminar connectivity remain unexplored.
source: While the computational properties of simplified circuits with multiple interneuron types have been investigated theoretically (Lee et al., 2017; Hertäg and Sprekeler, 2019; Garcia Del Molino et al., 2017; Lee, 2018), in the context of vision, locomotion, prediction errors, and whole-brain models (Lee and Mihalas, 2017; Dipoppa et al., 2018; Hertäg and Sprekeler, 2020; Bensaid et al., 2019), the dynamics of more complex networks comprising multiple layers with translaminar connectivity remain unexplored.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in the literature based on citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: It is unclear how firing rate descriptions of microcircuit function relate to oscillatory behavior of cortical networks, which can differ across cortical layers.
source: Moreover, even though models have examined the emergence of oscillations in local (Lee, 2018; Domhof and Tiesinga, 2021; Veit et al., 2017) and whole-brain neuronal networks (Bensaid et al., 2019) composed of canonical microcircuits, it is unclear how firing rate descriptions of microcircuit function relate to oscillatory behavior of cortical networks, which can differ across cortical layers (Bastos et al., 2018; Adesnik, 2018; van Kerkoerle et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in understanding based on citations to previous studies.

claim: The most comprehensive connectivity diagram to date for the primary mouse visual cortex is available from Jiang et al., 2015.
source: To address these questions, we take a computational approach and isolate the role of different neurons in rate- and oscillation-based functioning of the layered microcircuit of the primary mouse visual cortex, for which the most comprehensive connectivity diagram to date is available (Jiang et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Jiang et al., 2015.

claim: The superficial and deep layers in the visual microcircuit can operate in two different states, triggered by the external activation of specific interneuron types and each with different excitation–inhibition balance.
source: We found that the superficial and deep layers in the visual microcircuit can operate in two different states, triggered by the external activation of specific interneuron types and each with different excitation–inhibition balance: An inhibition dominated state controlled by SST neurons (SST state) and a disinhibited state that is attained by activation of PV and/or VIP neurons (PV/VIP states).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the modeling study.

claim: Disparities in recurrent connections within inhibitory cell classes play a crucial role for the different EI balance in the two states.
source: By perturbing connections of different types of interneurons, we confirmed that disparities in recurrent connections within these inhibitory cell classes play a crucial role for the different EI balance in the two states.
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling study based on perturbation experiments.

claim: Two mutual inhibitory motifs that include SST, PV, and VIP cells serve as ultrasensitive or bistable switches with different sensitivity.
source: Two mutual inhibitory motifs that include SST, PV, and VIP cells serve as ultrasensitive or bistable switches with different sensitivity, which can toggle the microcircuit between the two states.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the modeling study.

claim: In the inhibited regime slow beta-band oscillations were more prevalent especially in the deep layer, whereas in the disinhibited state fast gamma oscillations emerged predominately in the superficial layer.
source: Notably, we also found that in the inhibited regime slow beta-band oscillations were more prevalent especially in the deep layer, whereas in the disinhibited state fast gamma oscillations emerged predominately in the superficial layer, similar to experimental observations (Bastos et al., 2018; van Kerkoerle et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling study that is consistent with experimental observations cited.

claim: The model network consists of two different layers (superficial and deep), representing L2/3 and L5 of the primary visual cortex.
source: This network consists of two different layers (superficial and deep), representing L2/3 and L5 of the primary visual cortex and each containing four different cell types that are connected within and between layers: excitatory pyramidal cells (PYR), and three different classes of inhibitory cells (PV, SST, and VIP).
evidence: This describes the structure of the computational model.

claim: The connectivity was corrected for the different prevalence of each cell type.
source: The connectivity was corrected for the different prevalence of each cell type (Jiang et al., 2015) and scaled with a global parameter (G) to approximate effective coupling changes (Deco et al., 2013; Jobst et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes a methodological approach in the model based on cited studies.

claim: A sharp increase in pyramidal, PV and VIP cell activity with G was followed by a rapid decrease of mean rates in both layers.
source: A sharp increase in pyramidal, PV and VIP cell activity with G was followed by a rapid decrease of mean rates in both layers (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 1C.

claim: SST neurons also behaved similar to PV and VIP cells, but both rise and decay in their activity were much slower.
source: SST neurons also behaved similar to PV and VIP cells, but both rise and decay in their activity were much slower.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations.

claim: The average firing rates of pyramidal and SST neurons were higher in the deeper layer, in accordance with experimental results in mice.
source: The average firing rates of pyramidal and SST neurons were higher in the deeper layer, in accordance with experimental results in mice (Sakata and Harris, 2009; Senzai et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a finding from the model that is consistent with experimental results cited.

claim: For G > 100, the dominant LFP frequency steadily decreased to a low gamma (~40 Hz, superficial layer) or low beta range (~15 Hz, deep layer) for G = 500.
source: For G > 100, the dominant LFP frequency steadily decreased to a low gamma (~40 Hz, superficial layer) or low beta range (~15 Hz, deep layer) for G = 500.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations about oscillation frequency.

claim: The frequency consistently remained higher in deep layers, consistent with recent experimental findings in mouse V1.
source: Interestingly, the frequency consistently remained higher in deep layers, consistent with recent experimental findings in mouse V1 (Adesnik, 2018).
evidence: This is a finding from the model that is consistent with experimental findings cited.

claim: High gamma frequencies (G < 250) were stronger in superficial layers, whereas the power of slower oscillations (G > 250) was higher in deep layers, in congruence with empirical mouse V1 findings.
source: Moreover, high gamma frequencies (G < 250) were stronger in superficial layers, whereas the power of slower oscillations (G > 250) was higher in deep layers (Figure 1G), in congruence with empirical mouse V1 findings (Senzai et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a finding from the model shown in Figure 1G that is consistent with experimental findings cited.

claim: Stronger excitation and disinhibition in the deep layer together with more inhibition in the superficial layer underlie the experimentally observed firing rate and oscillation power differences between deep and superficial layers.
source: Thus, our model suggests that stronger excitation and disinhibition in the deep layer together with more inhibition in the superficial layer underlie the experimentally observed firing rate and oscillation power differences between deep and superficial layers.
evidence: This is an inference from the model based on connection manipulation experiments.

claim: Knocking out PV cells was accompanied by a slow oscillation (~30 Hz) in both layers with a frequency that remained approximately stable with G.
source: Knocking out PV cells was accompanied by a slow oscillation (~30 Hz) in both layers with a frequency that remained approximately stable with G.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations with PV cell silencing.

claim: When SST cells were removed the network oscillated at high frequency (~110 Hz) across all tested values of G.
source: By contrast, when SST cells were removed the network oscillated at high frequency (~110 Hz) across all tested values of G (Figure 2F, top, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, left).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations with SST cell silencing shown in figures.

claim: Oscillatory power was overall higher in the PV knockout case with a low frequency and lower in the SST silenced network with faster oscillations across all tested values of G.
source: Importantly, oscillatory power was overall higher in the PV knockout case with a low frequency and lower in the SST silenced network with faster oscillations across all tested values of G (Figure 2F, bottom, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, right).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations with cell silencing shown in figures.

claim: The relative dominance of PV and SST cell activity is an important factor that determines the oscillation frequency and power.
source: Thus, the relative dominance of PV and SST cell activity is an important factor that determines the oscillation frequency and power, which are inversely related in the full model (see below), but positively correlated in the partly silenced network.
evidence: This is an inference from the model simulations with cell silencing.

claim: SST cells exhibit reciprocal inhibitory connections with PV cells and also VIP cells in each layer, which brings these cell pairs in competition with each other.
source: SST cells exhibit reciprocal inhibitory connections with PV cells and also VIP cells in each layer, which brings these cell pairs in competition with each other (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the connectivity structure in the model shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Input to VIP or PV cells can suppress SST activity.
source: To verify this hypothesis, we first tested whether input to VIP or PV cells can suppress SST activity.
evidence: This is a hypothesis tested in the model simulations.

claim: As G increased, the responses of SST cells became more switch like with sigmoidal curves in both layers, a hallmark of an ultrasensitive switch in many biological systems.
source: Second, as G increased, the responses of SST cells became more switch like with sigmoidal curves in both layers, a hallmark of an ultrasensitive switch in many biological systems (Ferrell and Ha, 2014; Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 3A, with reference to biological systems.

claim: A similar sigmoidal decrease in SST firing rates with initial PYR disinhibition followed by inhibition was observed in both layers when only PV cells were driven.
source: A similar sigmoidal decrease in SST firing rates with initial PYR disinhibition followed by inhibition was observed in both layers when only PV cells were driven (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in figures.

claim: Hysteresis appeared at sufficiently high G values, as visible by the appearance of noncongruent response curves for the up and down direction in all cell types of both layers for VIP and PV input.
source: We found that hysteresis appeared at sufficiently high G values, as visible by the appearance of noncongruent response curves for the up and down direction in all cell types of both layers for VIP (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 3A) and PV input (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in figures.

claim: Inhibition-based ultrasensitivity and hysteresis commonly require strong inhibitory interactions between the components of the system.
source: Inhibition-based ultrasensitivity and hysteresis commonly require strong inhibitory interactions between the components of the system (Ferrell, 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ferrell, 2002.

claim: Selectively increasing the mutual inhibitory connections between SST <> VIP and SST <> PV cells was sufficient for ultrasensitivity and hysteresis to appear in the microcircuit.
source: Indeed, selectively increasing these weights was sufficient for ultrasensitivity and hysteresis to appear in the microcircuit (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in a figure supplement.

claim: Both nH and h increased monotonically with G when either VIP cells or PV cells were stimulated.
source: We found that both nH and h increased monotonically with G when either VIP cells (Figure 4A) or PV cells (Figure 4B) were stimulated.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: The addition of noise does not change the switching dynamics results.
source: We found that the addition of noise does not change the results (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a finding from robustness testing shown in a figure supplement.

claim: The jitter in the connection weights changed the slope of the SST response curves.
source: The jitter in the connection weights indeed changed the slope of the SST response curves (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B), which resulted in a large variety of Hill coefficient values (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is a finding from robustness testing shown in figure supplements.

claim: Both input to VIP and PV cells strongly increased the frequency of the dominant oscillation in superficial and deep layers, whereas the power of the oscillation peak generally decreased.
source: Both input to VIP and PV cells strongly increased the frequency of the dominant oscillation in superficial and deep layers, whereas the power of the oscillation peak generally decreased (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 5A-D.

claim: A marked transition between a slow and fast oscillation state was still visible, even when the time constant across all neurons was the same.
source: Remarkably, a marked transition between a slow and fast oscillation state was still visible, even when the time constant across all neurons was the same.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations with varied time constants.

claim: Driving SST cells resulted in a monotonic decay of activity of all other cell types in both layers for different values of G, in line with several experimental studies.
source: Driving SST cells resulted in a monotonic decay of activity of all other cell types in both layers for different values of G (Figure 6B), in line with several experimental studies (Chen, 2017; Dipoppa et al., 2018; Adesnik et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 6B that is consistent with experimental studies cited.

claim: Stimulation of SST cells reduced the frequency of oscillations.
source: Stimulation of SST cells also reduced the frequency of oscillations (Figure 6C–E).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 6C-E.

claim: As input to SST cells increased, the power of oscillations initially increased and subsequently decreased once PV cells were strongly suppressed.
source: However, as we increased the input to SST cells the power of oscillations initially increased and subsequently decreased once PV cells were strongly suppressed.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations.

claim: This finding replicates experimental results, in which stronger surround suppression is followed by a sudden transition from high frequency (gamma range) to lower frequency oscillations (high beta, low gamma range) and a concomitant increase in oscillatory power in mouse V1.
source: This finding replicates experimental results, in which stronger surround suppression is followed by a sudden transition from high frequency (gamma range) to lower frequency oscillations (high beta, low gamma range) and a concomitant increase in oscillatory power in mouse V1 (Chen, 2017; Veit et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement connects the model finding to experimental results cited.

claim: Stimulation of PYR cells strongly increased SST activity in both layers.
source: In this case, PYR input strongly increased SST activity (Figure 7A) (and to a lesser extent PV rates, see Figure 7—figure supplement 1B) in both layers, while VIP cells were suppressed (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in figures.

claim: Sufficiently high PYR input and G value caused a jump back to higher SST activity in both layers when VIP cells received a constant external input.
source: In this case, sufficiently high PYR input and G value caused a jump back to higher SST activity in both layers (Figure 7B) with a sudden suppression of PV and VIP activity (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in figures.

claim: These findings are consistent with recent optogenetic experiments in which strong PYR drive was associated with high SST activity and comparatively low PV rates.
source: These findings are consistent with recent optogenetic experiments in which strong PYR drive was associated with high SST activity and comparatively low PV rates (Hakim et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement connects the model findings to experimental results cited.

claim: The switching dynamics was preserved even in the absence of recurrent excitation, highlighting the fact that the switch is implemented by interactions among the three inhibitory neurons types.
source: Surprisingly, the switching dynamics was preserved even in the absence of recurrent excitation, highlighting the fact that the switch is implemented by interactions among the three inhibitory neurons types.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations with manipulated recurrent excitation.

claim: Input to VIP cells in the superficial layer showed a disinhibitory PYR rate increase in the deep layer, which was mainly due to a translaminar reduction of SST activity rather than a direct drive from superficial to deep PYR cells.
source: When the circuit displayed high SST activity, input to VIP cells in the superficial layer showed a disinhibitory PYR rate increase in the deep layer, which was mainly due to a translaminar reduction of SST activity rather than a direct drive from superficial to deep PYR cells (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Transitions between disinhibited and inhibited states triggered in one layer can propagate to the opposite layer and this interlayer interaction is primarily governed by translaminar SST connections.
source: In summary, these results demonstrate that transitions between disinhibited and inhibited states triggered in one layer can propagate to the opposite layer and this interlayer interaction is primarily governed by translaminar SST connections.
evidence: This is an inference from the model simulations with translaminar connection manipulations.

claim: L4 preferentially drives PYR and PV cells in superficial layers.
source: The extent of this drive through PYR cells is cell specific, as for instance L4 preferentially drives PYR and PV cells in superficial layers (Adesnik et al., 2012), while feedback input from the anterior cingulate cortex mostly targets VIP cells (Zhang et al., 2014; Figure 9A).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Adesnik et al., 2012 and Zhang et al., 2014.

claim: Feedback input from the anterior cingulate cortex mostly targets VIP cells.
source: The extent of this drive through PYR cells is cell specific, as for instance L4 preferentially drives PYR and PV cells in superficial layers (Adesnik et al., 2012), while feedback input from the anterior cingulate cortex mostly targets VIP cells (Zhang et al., 2014; Figure 9A).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2014.

claim: For small G values all cell types enhanced their activity for both feedforward and feedback types of drive, while there was a gradual suppression of SST cells for larger values.
source: For small G values all cell types enhanced their activity for both types of drive, while we found a gradual suppression of SST cells for larger values (Figure 9B, C).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 9B and 9C.

claim: In both feedforward and feedback input models, a suppression of the spontaneous low-frequency oscillation and a corresponding enhancement of higher frequency oscillations was observed due to strong PV and VIP activation.
source: In both input models we observed a suppression of the spontaneous low-frequency oscillation and a corresponding enhancement of higher frequency oscillations due to strong PV and VIP activation (Figure 9D).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 9D.

claim: These results are consistent with the experimental literature, which reported alpha oscillation suppression and gamma oscillation enhancement upon both visual stimulation and feedback associated visual attention.
source: These results are consistent with the experimental literature, which reported alpha oscillation suppression and gamma oscillation enhancement upon both visual stimulation (van Kerkoerle et al., 2014) and feedback associated visual attention (Klimesch, 2012).
evidence: This statement connects the model findings to experimental results cited.

claim: There is a strong asymmetry between recurrent connections among PV and SST cells: connections between PV cells in each layer are the strongest within the entire matrix, while recurrent connections among SST cells are entirely absent.
source: To this end, we examined the mouse V1 connectivity matrix and found that there is a strong asymmetry between recurrent connections among PV and SST cells. While connections between PV cells in each layer are the strongest within the entire matrix, recurrent connections among SST cells are entirely absent (Figure 10A, Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: This is an observation from the connectivity matrix shown in Figure 10A and Supplementary file 1d.

claim: The strong self-inhibition of PV cells effectively reduces their inhibitory effect on PYR cells, while SST cells can elicit comparatively stronger inhibition on PYR cells due to the absence of self-inhibition.
source: Thus, we hypothesized that the strong self-inhibition of PV cells effectively reduces their inhibitory effect on PYR cells, while SST cells can elicit comparatively stronger inhibition on PYR cells due to the absence of self-inhibition.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the connectivity structure.

claim: Exchanging the recurrent connections between PV and SST cells inverted their role in microcircuit state switching.
source: If this was true, exchanging the recurrent connections, that is removing PV self-connections and add them to SST cells may invert their role in microcircuit state switching (Figure 10A). In simulations with the inverted connectivity scheme we found that input to SST cells indeed created a disinhibition peak in the PYR cell response (Figure 10B, left), similar to VIP input in the original connectivity scheme (Figure 3A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), while PV and VIP cells showed a monotonic suppression (Figure 10B, right, Figure 10—figure supplements 1 and 2A).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations with modified connectivity shown in figures.

claim: Inhibitory state-dependent alterations in excitation–inhibition balance, which are at the core of the switching properties of the microcircuit, are due to large differences in PV and SST self-connectivity.
source: These results indeed suggest that inhibitory state-dependent alterations in excitation–inhibition balance, which are at the core of the switching properties of the microcircuit, are due to large differences in PV and SST self-connectivity (Figure 10E).
evidence: This is an inference from the model simulations with modified connectivity.

claim: Superficial and deep layers of the mouse V1 microcircuit are endowed with two switch mechanisms that can toggle the pyramidal cells between high (disinhibited) and low activity states (inhibited) across superficial and deep layers.
source: In this study, we showed that superficial and deep layers of the mouse V1 microcircuit are endowed with two switch mechanisms that can toggle the pyramidal cells (output of the microcircuit) between high (disinhibited) and low activity states (inhibited) across superficial and deep layers (Figure 10F).
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from the study shown in Figure 10F.

claim: The underlying switching mechanics are realized by the interactions among the three interneuron types (PV, SST, and VIP), which compete for inhibitory influence on pyramidal cells.
source: The underlying switching mechanics are realized by the interactions among the three interneuron types (PV, SST, and VIP), which compete for inhibitory influence on pyramidal cells.
evidence: This is an inference from the model simulations.

claim: In the inhibited state, SST cells dominate inhibition which serve as 'master regulators' by strongly connecting and inhibiting activity of pyramidal cells and other interneurons in the circuit.
source: In the inhibited state, SST cells dominate inhibition which serve as 'master regulators' by strongly connecting and inhibiting activity of pyramidal cells and other interneurons in the circuit (Jiang et al., 2015; Chen, 2017; Fino and Yuste, 2011; Urban-Ciecko and Barth, 2016; Naka et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference from the model supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: In the disinhibited state, excitation is mainly balanced by PV cells and to a lesser extent by VIP neurons, whereas SST activity is reduced.
source: In the disinhibited state, excitation is mainly balanced by PV cells (Ferguson and Gao, 2018) and to a lesser extent by VIP neurons (Garcia-Junco-Clemente et al., 2017), whereas SST activity is reduced.
evidence: This is an inference from the model supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Disinhibition through SST suppression was previously shown experimentally and theoretically.
source: While disinhibition through SST suppression was previously shown experimentally and theoretically (Pi et al., 2013; Walker et al., 2016; Hertäg and Sprekeler, 2019; Wang and Yang, 2018), the question remains why SST cells provide more inhibition than PV or VIP cells, even though the weights of the PV to PYR connections by far outweigh SST to PYR connections (Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to experimental and theoretical studies.

claim: Similar to previous simulations of anatomically simplified neuronal networks, self-inhibition of PV cells reduced their impact on PYR cells and enhanced PYR rates.
source: Similar to previous simulations of anatomically simplified neuronal networks (Hertäg and Sprekeler, 2019), we found that a key to this inhibitory asymmetry lies in the degree to which PV and SST cells are connected among themselves. While SST cells lack mutual connectivity, PV cells have strong mutual connectivity (that may also be reinforced by gap junctions Pfeffer et al., 2013; Jiang et al., 2015; Bartos et al., 2007). In our rate model, self-inhibition of PV cells reduced their impact on PYR cells and enhanced PYR rates.
evidence: This is a finding from the model that is consistent with previous simulations cited.

claim: A similar effect was found in spiking network models, where PV interactions enhanced PYR rates and synchrony.
source: We note that a similar effect was found in spiking network models, where PV interactions enhanced PYR rates and synchrony (Hahn et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a spiking network model study.

claim: The switching mechanism emerges as a consequence of two mutual inhibitory connection motifs from SST to PV and VIP, and PV/VIP to SST neurons, in both layers.
source: The switching mechanism emerges as a consequence of two mutual inhibitory connection motifs that is from SST to PV and VIP, and PV/VIP to SST neurons, in both layers.
evidence: This is an inference from the model about the mechanism of switching.

claim: The nature of the switch depended on the mutual inhibitory connectivity strength, rendering the state transition purely ultrasensitive with sigmoidal input–output curves for weaker weights or bistable with hysteresis and memory for stronger weights.
source: The nature of this switch depended on the mutual inhibitory connectivity strength, rendering the state transition purely ultrasensitive with sigmoidal input–output curves for weaker weights or bistable with hysteresis and memory for stronger weights, consistent with recent observations made in simplified inhibitory neuronal networks (Hertäg and Sprekeler, 2019).
evidence: This is a finding from the model that is consistent with previous observations cited.

claim: Switching based on double negative feedback has been conserved during evolution in many biological systems.
source: Switching based on double negative feedback has been conserved during evolution in many biological systems (Ferrell and Ha, 2014; Ferrell, 2002; Tyson et al., 2003) and we found that it may also be a hallmark of cortical microcircuits.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to studies on biological systems.

claim: The two ways to control the switch differ in their sensitivity, with VIP cells requiring considerably less input to control SST activity and flip the circuit to the disinhibited state in both layers than PV cells.
source: Notably, the two ways to control the switch differ in their sensitivity, with VIP cells requiring considerably less input to control SST activity and flip the circuit to the disinhibited state in both layers than PV cells.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations.

claim: PV cells seem to be more specialized in keeping the excitation–inhibition balance at sufficiently high levels, whereas VIP cells play more a switching role, even though both cell types can assume both functions.
source: Thus, PV cells seem to be more specialized in keeping the excitation–inhibition balance at sufficiently high levels, whereas VIP cells play more a switching role, even though both cell types can assume both functions.
evidence: This is an inference from the model simulations.

claim: Each layer can transmit its state change to the other through translaminar connectivity, and effectively synchronize inhibited or disinhibited states across the whole microcircuit.
source: The switching circuitry of the microcircuit can not only be activated by simultaneous input to superficial and deep layers, but each layer can transmit its state change to the other through translaminar connectivity, and effectively synchronize inhibited or disinhibited states across the whole microcircuit.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations.

claim: The two-layer microcircuit as a whole can act as a switch, whose state may be used to guide activity flow of pyramidal cells in the feedforward (via L2/3) and feedback direction (L5).
source: These results suggest that the two-layer microcircuit as a whole can act as a switch, whose state may be used to guide activity flow of pyramidal cells in the feedforward (via L2/3) and feedback direction (L5) (Markov et al., 2014b; Markov et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is an inference from the model supported by citations.

claim: The presence of bistability based on mutual inhibitory connection motifs provides an alternative to the dominant view that persistent transitions between low and high firing rate states across the brain are primarily based on local or interareal recurrent connectivity between excitatory neurons.
source: The presence of bistability based on mutual inhibitory connection motifs also provides an alternative to the dominant view that persistent transitions between low and high firing rate states across the brain (Christophel et al., 2017), which underlie working memory required for attention (Ardid et al., 2014), consciousness (Dehaene et al., 2014; Dehaene and Changeux, 2011; van Vugt et al., 2018), and language processing (Kunze et al., 2017; Nelson et al., 2017; Pallier et al., 2011), are primarily based on local (Compte et al., 2000) or interareal (Dehaene et al., 2014; van Vugt et al., 2018) recurrent connectivity between excitatory neurons.
evidence: This is an inference from the model supported by citations to studies on persistent states.

claim: Bistability is controlled by properties of local inhibitory connectivity, opening up the possibility that anatomical heterogeneity and gradients across the brain may reflect the presence of bistable switches in some brain areas and ultrasensitive switches without memory in other regions.
source: In our study, bistability is controlled by properties of local inhibitory connectivity, opening up the possibility that anatomical heterogeneity and gradients across the brain may reflect the presence of bistable switches in some brain areas and ultrasensitive switches without memory in other regions (Kim et al., 2017; Fulcher et al., 2019; Demirtaş et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference from the model supported by citations to studies on brain heterogeneity.

claim: Two negative feedback loops between pyramidal cells and interneurons endow both deep and superficial layers with an intrinsic oscillation.
source: Two negative feedback loops between pyramidal cells and interneurons endow both deep and superficial layers with an intrinsic oscillation.
evidence: This is an inference from the model about the mechanism of oscillations.

claim: Consistent with experiments and models, PV cells drive high frequencies ('gamma range'), whereas SST cells prefer lower frequencies ('beta range').
source: Consistent with experiments and models, PV cells drive high frequencies ('gamma range'), whereas SST cells prefer lower frequencies ('beta range') (Cardin et al., 2009; Chen, 2017; Lee, 2018).
evidence: This is a finding from the model that is consistent with experiments and models cited.

claim: During the inhibited switch state the dominating SST cells impose a slower frequency on PYR cells as compared to the PV dominated disinhibition state with high frequencies.
source: Accordingly, during the inhibited switch state the dominating SST cells impose a slower frequency on PYR cells as compared to the PV dominated disinhibition state with high frequencies.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations.

claim: VIP cells had little influence on oscillation frequency.
source: VIP cells had little influence on oscillation frequency.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations.

claim: The switch in frequency is already shaped by the connectivity pattern of the circuit and is only partly modified by intrinsic neuronal properties such as differing time constants.
source: An interesting finding of our study is that this switch in frequency is already shaped by the connectivity pattern of the circuit and is only partly modified by intrinsic neuronal properties such as differing time constants.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations with varied time constants.

claim: In the absence of noise and oscillations, the ability of the network to change its frequency is not dependent on the exact time constant of neuron populations suggesting that the switch is already engrained in the connectivity.
source: Note also that in the absence of noise and oscillations, the ability of the network to change its frequency is not dependent on the exact time constant of neuron populations suggesting that the switch is already engrained in the connectivity.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations.

claim: Neuron population time constants determine the amount of change in the oscillation frequency as the network goes from SST to PV mode.
source: Neuron population time constants, however, do determine the amount of change in the oscillation frequency as the network goes from SST to PV mode.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations with varied time constants.

claim: This result provides a potential explanation for a longstanding question of what determines the oscillation frequency in neuronal circuits.
source: This result thus provides a potential explanation for a longstanding question of what determines the oscillation frequency in neuronal circuits (Brunel and Wang, 2003; Jia et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference from the model supported by citations to studies on oscillation frequency.

claim: This finding is in contrast to previous modeling efforts which introduced slow and high frequencies by endowing interneurons with different time constants.
source: This finding is in contrast to previous modeling efforts which introduced slow and high frequencies by endowing interneurons with different time constants (Hyafil et al., 2015; Mejias et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement contrasts the current findings with previous modeling approaches cited.

claim: Animal experiments have revealed that the power of high-frequency oscillations was stronger in the superficial layer, while slower oscillation had more power in the deep layers.
source: Animal experiments have revealed that the power of high-frequency oscillations was stronger in the superficial layer, while slower oscillation had more power in the deep layers (van Kerkoerle et al., 2014; Haegens, 2015; Buffalo et al., 2011; Bonaiuto et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The emergence of differences in oscillations in deep and superficial layers crucially depends on specific anatomical connections.
source: Based on our results we argue that the emergence of such differences in oscillations in deep and superficial layers crucially depends on specific anatomical connections (see Figure 2A).
evidence: This is an inference from the model simulations shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Visual stimulation mediated by feedforward connections and visual attention mediated by feedback connections suppress slow oscillations (alpha band) and enhance fast oscillations in the gamma band.
source: Moreover, our results also replicate experimental findings which have shown that visual stimulation mediated by feedforward connections and visual attention mediated by feedback connections suppress slow oscillations (alpha band) and enhance fast oscillations in the gamma band (van Kerkoerle et al., 2014; Klimesch, 2012).
evidence: This statement connects the model findings to experimental results cited.

claim: The results suggest an alternative, anatomically based taxonomy for oscillations, dividing them into competing SST- (low frequency) and PV-driven rhythms (high frequency).
source: Thus, our results also suggest an alternative, anatomically based taxonomy for oscillations, dividing them into competing SST- (low frequency) and PV-driven rhythms (high frequency).
evidence: This is an inference from the model simulations.

claim: During the transition between (PV or SST dominated) switch states the oscillation frequency and power behave asymmetrically, that is an increase in frequency is accompanied by a decrease in power.
source: Notably, during the transition between (PV or SST dominated) switch states the oscillation frequency and power behave asymmetrically, that is an increase in frequency is accompanied by a decrease in power.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations.

claim: When PV or SST cells are strongly suppressed or silenced, frequency and power change symmetrically.
source: However, when PV or SST cells are strongly suppressed or silenced, frequency and power change symmetrically.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations with cell silencing.

claim: A decrease in frequency and increase in power is found in recent experiments in monkeys and mice, in which small stimuli trigger a high-frequency oscillation (~60 Hz) that is replaced by a lower frequency (~30 Hz) in the presence of larger stimuli.
source: A decrease in frequency and increase in power is also found in recent experiments in monkeys and mice, in which small stimuli trigger a high-frequency oscillation (~60 Hz) that is replaced by a lower frequency (~30 Hz) in the presence of larger stimuli (Chen, 2017; Veit et al., 2017; Gieselmann and Thiele, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Anatomical studies show that surround suppression effect is presumably mediated by lateral excitatory input from the surround to SST neurons in the center.
source: Anatomical studies show that this surround suppression effect is presumably mediated by lateral excitatory input from the surround to SST neurons in the center (Adesnik et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to an anatomical study.

claim: The model suggests that the surround switches the microcircuit from a PV/VIP dominated state with a high frequency, putatively mediated by stimulus triggered feedforward and feedback drive, to a more inhibited state caused by enhanced lateral drive to SST cells.
source: Our model suggests that the surround switches the microcircuit from a PV/VIP dominated state with a high frequency, putatively mediated by stimulus triggered feedforward and feedback drive (Zhang et al., 2014; Gonchar and Burkhalter, 2003), to a more inhibited state caused by enhanced lateral drive to SST cells.
evidence: This is an inference from the model supported by citations.

claim: Experiments have also reported the inverse case with an increase in oscillation frequency and decrease in power after enhancing visual stimulus contrast.
source: We note that experiments have also reported the inverse case with an increase in oscillation frequency and decrease in power after enhancing visual stimulus contrast (Ray and Maunsell, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to an experimental study.

claim: The coupling parameter G can be related to the overall cell count in the studied circuits.
source: The switching properties in the model depend on the coupling parameter G, which scales the overall connectivity between neurons of the circuit. This parameter has been previously used to study whole-brain models of cortical dynamics (Deco et al., 2013) and can be related to the overall cell count in the studied circuits.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Feedforward and feedback input lead to suppression of SST and PYR activity for sufficiently high G values, which is inconsistent with recent experimental results in mouse V1, where the rate of all cell types increased after visual stimulation.
source: We found that feedforward and feedback input lead to suppression of SST and PYR activity for sufficiently high G values. This is inconsistent with recent experimental results in mouse V1, where the rate of all cell types increased after visual stimulation (Dipoppa et al., 2018; Kirchberger et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a finding from the model that is inconsistent with experimental results cited.

claim: Smaller values of G may be biologically more realistic for mouse V1.
source: This suggests that smaller values of G may be biologically more realistic for mouse V1.
evidence: This is an inference from the comparison of model results with experimental data.

claim: The connectivity matrix used in the model is based on the detailed anatomical study of Jiang et al., 2015, which did not capture layers 4 and 6 of mouse V1.
source: The connectivity matrix used in the model is based on the detailed anatomical study of Jiang et al., 2015, which did not capture layers 4 and 6 of mouse V1.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the model based on the source of connectivity data.

claim: There is limited anatomical knowledge about the cell-specific connectivity within layers 4 and 6 and their connections to other layers in the microcircuit.
source: There exist a number of studies which have charted the different morphological and biochemical cell types in these two layers, which can also be divided into PV, SST, and VIP classes similar to layers 2/3 and 5 in the present study (Scala et al., 2019; Frandolig et al., 2019; Yavorska and Wehr, 2021; Ding et al., 2021). However, there is limited anatomical knowledge about the cell-specific connectivity within each layer and their connections to other layers in the microcircuit.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to studies on cell types and identifies a gap in knowledge.

claim: The disinhibited state of the switch naturally entails the risk of runaway excitation.
source: The disinhibited state of the switch naturally entails the risk of runaway excitation.
evidence: This is an inference about the potential consequences of the disinhibited state.

claim: The microcircuit contains supplementary homeostatic mechanisms that keep disinhibition within healthy boundaries.
source: Our results provide evidence that the microcircuit contains supplementary homeostatic mechanisms that keep disinhibition within healthy boundaries.
evidence: This is an inference from the model simulations.

claim: When the circuit is disinhibited and SST activity suppressed, strong drive to pyramidal cell can cause a sudden reversal of SST neurons to a high firing rate state and thereby restore a more inhibited state in the microcircuit.
source: When the circuit is disinhibited and SST activity suppressed, strong drive to pyramidal cell can cause a sudden reversal of SST neurons to a high firing rate state and thereby restore a more inhibited state in the microcircuit.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations.

claim: This phenomenon was reported experimentally and in a recent theoretical study showing elevated visually evoked SST rates, after prior suppression through VIP cells during darkness.
source: This phenomenon was reported experimentally (Pakan et al., 2016) and in a recent theoretical study (Garcia Del Molino et al., 2017) showing elevated visually evoked SST rates, after prior suppression through VIP cells during darkness.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to experimental and theoretical studies.

claim: The model replicates some of the experimental findings obtained from monkey V1 recordings, including the prevalence of gamma oscillations in the superficial layers and stronger power of slow frequency oscillations in deep layers.
source: While our results were obtained using anatomical data from mouse V1, the model also replicates some of the experimental findings obtained from monkey V1 recordings. Notably, the prevalence of gamma oscillations in the superficial layers and stronger power of slow frequency oscillations in deep layers has been reported by several studies (van Kerkoerle et al., 2014; Haegens, 2015; Buffalo et al., 2011; Bonaiuto et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement connects the model findings to experimental results in monkeys cited.

claim: The abrupt transition from high frequency to slow frequency oscillations due to increase in visual stimulus size and associated surround suppression size is a classic finding in monkey V1.
source: Moreover, the abrupt transition from high frequency to slow frequency oscillations due to increase in visual stimulus size and associated surround suppression size is a classic finding in monkey V1 (Gieselmann and Thiele, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to an experimental study in monkeys.

claim: Despite the lack of cell type-specific anatomical knowledge in the monkey primary visual cortex, the results suggest that the canonical microcircuit of both species may share common principles.
source: Despite the lack of cell type-specific anatomical knowledge in the monkey primary visual cortex (Vanni et al., 2021), these results suggest that the canonical microcircuit of both species may share common principles.
evidence: This is an inference from the model supported by a citation about anatomical knowledge.

claim: Asymmetric changes in oscillation frequency and power are abolished with silencing of PV or SST cells.
source: We found that asymmetric changes in oscillation frequency and power are abolished with silencing of PV or SST cells, a result that can be experimentally tested.
evidence: This is a finding from the model that is presented as a testable prediction.

claim: The model predicts that driving PYR cells is followed by linear or nonlinear responses in inhibitory cells depending on the dominance of SST or PV/VIP cells, respectively.
source: Moreover, our model predicts that driving PYR cells is followed by linear or nonlinear responses in inhibitory cells depending on the dominance of SST or PV/VIP cells, respectively.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model.

claim: Experiments could test whether inhibition or disinhibition mediated by driving specific inhibitory cells in one layer propagate to the other layer.
source: Finally, experiments could test whether inhibition or disinhibition mediated by driving specific inhibitory cells in one layer propagate to the other layer, as our simulations showed.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model that can be experimentally tested.

claim: The microcircuit function that emerges from the computational study is a homeostatic switch that toggles pyramidal cells between an inhibited and disinhibited state.
source: In conclusion, the microcircuit function that emerges from our computational study is a homeostatic switch that toggles pyramidal cells, the principal output neurons of the circuit, between an inhibited and disinhibited state.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from the study.

claim: The switching dynamics is orchestrated by an array of inhibitory neurons, each performing a specific task in the switch mechanics.
source: The switching dynamics is orchestrated by an array of inhibitory neurons, each performing a specific task in the switch mechanics.
evidence: This is an inference from the model simulations.

claim: Feedforward, feedback, and lateral input may change the position of the switch and regulate the flow of excitation to downstream microcircuits.
source: Feedforward, feedback, and lateral input may change the position of the switch and regulate the flow of excitation to downstream microcircuits (Cardin, 2018; Fishell and Kepecs, 2020; Hahn et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference from the model supported by citations.

claim: The results map different types of oscillations onto different interneuron types and link them with distinct switch states.
source: Our results also map different types of oscillations onto different interneuron types and link them with distinct switch states, which in the future may help to bring together rate- and oscillation-based experimental paradigms.
evidence: This is an inference from the model about the implications of the findings.

claim: The results provide mechanistic insight into the long held notion that slow oscillations assume an inhibitory function, while fast oscillations serve information processing.
source: They also provide mechanistic insight into the long held notion that slow oscillations assume an inhibitory function, while fast oscillations serve information processing (Hahn et al., 2021; Klimesch et al., 2007; Jensen and Mazaheri, 2010; Singer, 1999; Fries, 2015).
evidence: This is an inference from the model supported by citations to studies on oscillation function.

claim: The model is based on pairwise connectivity between major neuron types in superficial and deep layers of the neocortex from Jiang et al., 2015.
source: In this study, we developed a firing rate model of the visual cortical microcircuit. This model is based on pairwise connectivity between major neuron types in superficial and deep layers of the neocortex (Jiang et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the basis of the computational model.

claim: Jiang et al., 2015 exhaustively mapped out the connectivity (EPSP and IPSP strength and connection probability) between a large number of morphologically defined neurons within and between layers 1, 2/3 (superficial), and 5 (deep) of the primary visual cortex of the mouse.
source: Using octuple whole-cell recordings, Jiang et al., 2015 exhaustively mapped out the connectivity (excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP) and inhibitory postsynaptic potential (IPSP) strength and connection probability) between a large number of morphologically defined neurons (interneurons and pyramidal cells) within and between layers 1, 2/3 (superficial), and 5 (deep) of the primary visual cortex of the mouse, while layers 4 and 6 were not included.
evidence: This describes the experimental basis of the connectivity data used in the model.

claim: Jiang et al., 2015 quantified the relative prevalence of each cell type and reported synaptic plasticity properties of specific connections.
source: In addition, Jiang et al., 2015 also quantified the relative prevalence of each cell type and reported synaptic plasticity properties of specific connections.
evidence: This describes additional data from Jiang et al., 2015 used in the model.

claim: Different interneurons were labeled as PV cells (layer 2/3: basket cells and chandelier cells; layer 5: shrub cells and horizontally elongated cells), SST cells (layers 2/3 and 5: Martinotti cells), and VIP cells (only layer 2/3: bitufted cells and bipolar cells) based on their genetic makeup.
source: Finally, based on their genetic makeup, different interneurons were labeled as PV cells (layer 2/3: basket cells and chandelier cells; layer 5: shrub cells and horizontally elongated cells), SST cells (layers 2/3 and 5: Martinotti cells), and VIP cells (only layer 2/3: bitufted cells and bipolar cells).
evidence: This describes the classification of interneurons used in the model.

claim: A single connectivity matrix (C) was created by element-wise multiplication of EPSP/IPSP strength (i.e., mean amplitude) and connection probability matrices.
source: To convert the original connectivity data (see Supplementary file 1a for the connection probability matrix and Supplementary file 1b for the weight [EPSP/IPSP] matrix) into a format suited for a computational model, we performed several manipulations. First, restricting our analysis to pyramidal cells and three major interneurons types (PV, SST, and VIP), we created a single connectivity matrix (C) by element-wise multiplication of EPSP/IPSP strength (i.e., mean amplitude) and connection probability matrices.
evidence: This describes a methodological step in creating the model.

claim: VIP neurons were divided into VIPsup and VIPdeep cell types based on their preferential targeting of other neurons in L2/3 or L5, even though both types were anatomically located in the superficial layer.
source: After inspection of the connectivity matrix, we noticed that out of the two existing VIP cell types, one VIP cell type preferentially targeted other neurons in L2/3 (bitufted cells), whereas the other only innervated L5 (bipolar cells). Based on this observation, we divided VIP neurons into VIPsup and VIPdeep cell types, even though both types were anatomically located in the superficial layer.
evidence: This describes a methodological decision in the model based on connectivity patterns.

claim: All inhibitory weights in the matrix were scaled down by a factor of 0.2 to account for the roughly five times more pyramidal neurons in a microcircuit than interneurons.
source: Thus, we had four neuron types in both deep and superficial layers. Instead of modeling populations of neurons with N cells for each class, we modeled each cell population using a single firing rate-based neuron. However, we adapted the connectivity weights according to their relative prevalence, which is computationally less expensive. To this end, we first followed the general rule that there are roughly five times more pyramidal neurons in a microcircuit than interneurons. Therefore, all inhibitory weights in the matrix were scaled down by a factor of 0.2.
evidence: This describes a methodological step in creating the model based on known cell prevalence.

claim: The weights of each interneuron type were multiplied with its relative prevalence.
source: Next, we multiplied the weights of each interneuron type with its relative prevalence (Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: This describes a methodological step in creating the model.

claim: Conduction delays were not modeled explicitly because distances within the microcircuit are very short.
source: Because distances within the microcircuit are very short, conduction delays were not modeled explicitly.
evidence: This describes a modeling decision based on the spatial scale of the circuit.

claim: The rate of pyramidal cells in each layer was used as a proxy for superficial and deep LFPs.
source: We used the rate of pyramidal cells in each layer as a proxy for superficial and deep LFPs and its oscillatory behavior was investigated as a function of external drive.
evidence: This describes a methodological approach in the model.

claim: Ultrasensitivity reflects the behavior of a system where small changes in input cause large changes in output and is observed in many natural systems such as biochemical reactions.
source: Ultrasensitivity reflects the behavior of a system where small changes in input cause large changes in output. Such behavior is observed in many natural systems such as biochemical reactions (Ferrell and Ha, 2014; Ferrell and Machleder, 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to studies on ultrasensitivity.

claim: Ultrasensitivity can be quantified by fitting a sigmoidal curve to the input–output transfer function using the Hill equation.
source: Ultrasensitivity can be quantified by fitting a sigmoidal curve to the input–output transfer function. Here, we used the Hill equation (Ferrell and Ha, 2014) to estimate the sensitivity of the output (y) to the input (x)
evidence: This describes a methodological approach supported by a citation.

claim: If the Hill coefficient n = 1, the Hill curve is hyperbolic, whereas n > 1 indicates a sigmoidal shape with growing slope (i.e., sensitivity) as n increases.
source: If n = 1, the Hill curve is hyperbolic, whereas n > 1 indicates a sigmoidal shape with growing slope (i.e., sensitivity) as n increases.
evidence: This describes the interpretation of the Hill coefficient.

claim: Hysteresis in general describes the dependence of a system's behavior on the past and implicates the presence of memory.
source: Hysteresis in general describes the dependence of a system's behavior on the past and implicates the presence of memory.
evidence: This is a general definition of hysteresis.

claim: In the presence of hysteresis, the response curves for increasing and decreasing input do not collapse.
source: In the presence of hysteresis, the response curves for increasing and decreasing input do not collapse.
evidence: This describes a characteristic of hysteresis.
